text: So we have talked about where this is going. Now let us talk about what any of these words actually mean, because the vocabulary in this field is a genuine mess, and knowing your way around it is worth more than it sounds.
It starts with a second post from Andrej Karpathy, written a good while before the one we looked at. This is the one where he coined the term vibe coding.

He described a new kind of coding, where you give in fully to the vibes, embrace the exponentials, and forget that the code even exists. His point was that the models had simply got too good to keep reading everything they wrote. You ask, you let it go, you come back and look at what it did.

And that post kicked off a year that was, honestly, an emotional rollercoaster for everyone doing this seriously. It is worth walking through, because you are going to feel every one of these stages yourself.

First came surprise. These things could do far more than anyone expected. Then denial, where a lot of people pushed back hard and insisted it was a parlour trick. Then astonishment, when they actually tried it themselves and watched it build something real.

Then frustration, when it turned out not to work as cleanly as the demos suggested. And then, genuinely, anger. There is a well known story of a developer getting so exasperated that he made the agent write performance reports on its own repeated mistakes, so it would have to read back what it kept getting wrong. That is the level of frustration we are talking about.

And then acceptance. The people using this every day started to learn where it is strong, where it is weak, and how to get the most out of it without walking into the same wall every afternoon. That is the stage this program is trying to get you to, quickly, without the year of pain.

And then something changed. Around the end of last year there was a genuine inflection point, with a run of much stronger models. Suddenly the repeated, maddening mistakes largely stopped. The agents got dramatically more trustworthy, and a huge wave of progress followed almost immediately.
That matters for you in a very practical way. If you tried this a year ago and gave up in disgust, the thing you gave up on no longer exists. It is worth coming back.
Now, the vocabulary. Three terms get used constantly, they overlap, and people mean different things by all three. Let us pin them down.

A vibe coder is Karpathy's original term. Sometimes people use it to mean a fairly amateur approach. Set something running, throw it away if it does not work, try again. And sometimes people use it to mean this entire field. Both usages are common, which is exactly the problem.

A vibe engineer is a term from the writer Simon Willison, and it means the professional side of the same thing. Building real software, to a real standard, but building it with agents. That is the shift we make in week two.
And an agentic coder is where the expert lands. Working with an agent as a genuine collaborator, a sidekick, or with several of them at once. That is week three.

And now the trap, because these words genuinely do point in two directions. If somebody says agentic coder, they might mean a person who codes with the help of agents, which is what we mean in this program. Or they might mean a person who builds agents, which is a completely different job.

It gets worse. People call the platforms themselves coding agents, because they are agents that write code. So the same phrase can be a person, or a product, depending on who is talking. There is no fixing this. The only real advice is that when it matters, just ask the person which one they mean.
Right. Vocabulary done. Let us talk about the tools, because there are only three shapes of tool in this entire field, and once you see the three, every product you meet slots into one of them.

The first shape is the I D E. An integrated development environment. A full application, with windows and menus and panes, and an agent living in a sidebar inside it. This is the most familiar shape if you have ever opened a code editor, and it is where we spent today.

The second shape is the plugin. Rather than a whole new application, you bolt the agent onto an editor you already use. Almost always that editor is Visual Studio Code, which is free, open source, and extremely widely used. Same agent, but it lives inside the thing you already had open.

And the third shape is the command line. The C L I. A terminal. Black background, text, no windows, no buttons. It looks like something from the nineteen eighties, and if you have never used one it looks actively hostile.

And here is the surprise. That third shape turned out to be the best one. It started almost by accident, as a side project that became Claude Code, and it blew up so completely that essentially every other company has since shipped one. Stepping back to a retro looking text interface turned out to be the most productive way to work with an agent, and by week two you will understand exactly why.

So here is the landscape, sorted into those three shapes. For I D Es, there is Cursor, Codex from OpenAI, Antigravity from Google, and Windsurf. For plugins, the one that dominates is GitHub Copilot, usually inside Visual Studio Code. And for the command line, there is Claude Code, plus Cursor's own, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, Amp, and more arriving constantly.

And one honest footnote, because the neat boxes leak. Claude Code also ships an extension for Visual Studio Code and for Cursor, which technically makes it a plugin as well. Do not let that bother you. It is primarily a command line tool, and that is how we will treat it.
Which brings us to the last thing, and it is the most useful habit you can build in this field. Separating signal from noise.

There is a genuine tsunami of announcements in this space. Every single day, social media is full of new tools, new frameworks, new claims that everything has changed again. Almost all of it will not matter in six weeks.

And occasionally, something lands that genuinely does change how everybody works. Claude Code was one of those. Telling those two apart, quickly, is a real skill, and it is the difference between staying current and spending your entire life reading launch posts. Focus on what actually holds up. Tomorrow, we go under the hood.
